name: Vocative Construction

1.definition: Addresses the hearer directly, identifying them as the intended recipient
1.details: Forms its own intonation phrase, typically with fall-rise or level contour; summons use may have high sustained "calling" contour. Not syntactically integrated as a clause argument. NP is either bare or determined by 1st/2nd person forms only (genitive my/our/your, or determinative you).

examples.note: Summons with calling contour (high sustained pitch)

constraints.description: NP is bare or determined only by 1st/2nd person forms (my, our, your, you); 3rd-person and non-deictic determiners excluded
Requires addressee to be present (real or imagined)
Forms separate intonation phrase with fall-rise, level, or calling contour
Can occur clause-initially, clause-medially, or clause-finally

1.notes: Vocatives strongly favour bare NPs, especially for proper names and kinship terms

relatedConstructions.notes: Addressee-directed packaging of the ostensive NP (securing the channel)
Only the summons/call use is exclamatory; tag and address vocatives are not
Vocative function licenses bare NP for kinship terms that would otherwise require determination
Proper names freely occur as vocatives

projection.target: An overt imperative subject and a vocative can co-occur, as in Lee, you take the first shift. Moving Lee to the end can preserve the address reading while you continues to supply the subject. The name in the vocative is therefore not the only potential subject expression.
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts vocatives and subjects in imperative clauses. The constructed position and co-occurrence test illustrates the proposed distribution without relying on corpus frequencies or kin-term acquisition claims.

diagnostics: kinship terms bare in vocative but determined elsewhere

stabilisers.evidence: Need to secure attention and identify addressee
High frequency of vocative proper names and kinship terms in child-directed speech
Early-acquired; vocative kinship terms among first multi-word uses

coupling.mechanism: Vocative use licenses bare form; bare form signals vocative construal

curious.title: Calling someone by name
curious.summary: A name or title said directly to the person you're speaking to, set apart from the rest of the sentence.
curious.body:
In Mom, can you help me?, the word Mom isn't part of what is being asked. It addresses the hearer directly and picks them out as the person meant. This is a vocative.

It sits in its own stretch of speech, with its own tone, such as a fall-rise, a level tone, or a high held calling tone when summoning someone. It can come at the start, the middle or the end: I think, Brett, you're wrong. The noun phrase is either bare, as in Mom or Ladies and gentlemen, or begins with my, our, your or you, as in My friend, let me explain. A drawn-out, high Moooom! is the calling version.

This dictionary marks this account as provisional.
curious.try: Think of how you get a friend's attention across a room. Do you say their name on its own, in a calling tone?

teacher.summary: Helps explain direct address, its separate intonation and the determiners it allows.
teacher.explain: A vocative addresses the hearer directly. It forms its own intonation phrase, with a fall-rise or level contour, or a high sustained calling contour for a summons. It is not selected by the verb and is not syntactically integrated as a clause argument. The noun phrase is either bare or determined only by first- and second-person forms (the genitives my, our, your, or the determinative you). It can occur clause-initially, clause-medially or clause-finally, and it needs an addressee, real or imagined. In an imperative, an overt subject and a vocative can co-occur, as in Lee, you take the first shift. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional.
teacher.terms: Genitive is used here for my, our and your, rather than possessive.

contrasts.text: Lee, you take the first shift.
contrasts.note: Vocative Lee, with you as the subject.

watch_for: A learner might treat the vocative as the subject of the clause, when in an imperative the vocative and an overt subject can co-occur.
A learner might read the vocative as part of the clause, when it forms its own intonation phrase.
teacher.activity: Students read a short dialogue aloud, first with vocatives placed at the start, then in the middle and at the end. They notice how the vocative is set apart from the rest of the sentence.

child.hook: When you call someone's name, what happens to your voice?
child.explain: When we speak straight to someone, we can say their name. Mom, can you help me? The name stands apart from the rest of the sentence.
child.play: Say the same sentence three times, with a friend's name at the start, middle and end. Does the name sound set apart each time?

checked.note: Fixed: curious list of forms no longer excludes bare noun phrases such as Ladies and gentlemen; replaced the 'pause on either side' and 'shouted' wording with the entry's contours (fall-rise, level, high sustained calling); removed the 'rising tone' option; child and teacher activities no longer rest on pauses; removed the unsupported 'noun of address' term and the punctuation-based watch_for. Dismissed: none. Second round: fixed teacher.terms by cutting 'Vocative is the traditional name' (this dictionary uses the label but makes no claim about its history).
